newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian grey economy equals 25 pct GDP-research.
newsitem.headline: Croatian grey economy equals 25 pct GDP-research.

text.p: Croatia's "grey economy" accounts for at least one quarter of the country's economic output, research ordered by the Finance Ministry and presented on Wednesday showed.

The 376-page report of research conducted by the government-funded Institute for Public Finances, said that at least 25 percent of Croatia's gross domestic product (GDP) was not covered by official statistics.
"We were not surprised by this figure, we even thought it would be higher," Finance Minister Bozo Prka told a presentation conference.

Croatia loses seven to eight billion kuna per year in budget revenues due to various forms of tax evasion and is determined to slash the amount of the grey economy to some 10 to 12 percent of GDP by 2000, Prka said.
Croatia's 1996 GDP was estimated at around 100 billion kuna ($18 bln).

"Some elements of the grey economy...are a useful part of the national economy," Prka told Reuters, referring to people who run businesses from home and do not pay rent as well as private food cultivation. "But tax evasion is certainly damaging because it makes the redistribution of the fiscal burden unjust, discriminating against those who do pay taxes," he said.

Prka said the Finance Ministry planned to slash the amount of untaxed economic activity by introducing value added tax as of January 1, 1998, and by improving financial controls as well as the legislation and efficiency of the judicial system.

The research places Croatia in the top half of a list of world economies with strong grey economies, together with most eastern and central European countries in transition, said Ivo Bicanic, one of the leaders of the project.

The authors singled out the high level of public spending -- the state spends some 52 percent of average Croatian revenues -- as the main factor forcing people to indulge in illegal economic activities.

Bicanic also mentioned the tradition of tax evasion during communism, poor business ethics, four years of war for independence that promoted smuggling and the transition from a state-planned to a market economy.

The size of the grey economy by sector varies from eight percent in industry to 68 percent in commerce, while the lack of comprehensive official statistics make estimates for tourism and construction more difficult.
